segments.narration: Scotland buried its finest rock art on purpose in 1965. A slab at Faifley, forty-two feet across, carved with about ninety cups and rings.
Bronze Age hands cut those spirals into the rock. Reverend James Harvey recorded the stone in 1887, and curious visitors never stopped arriving.
Then came the graffiti, scratched right beside the prehistoric carvings. Why would anyone protect a masterpiece by hiding it under earth completely?
One archaeologist had already made things worse. In 1937 Ludovic Mann painted bright lines across the carvings to test an eclipse-prediction theory.
Mann's own measurements disproved him. Glasgow archaeologists re-exposed the slab in 2016, scanned every groove in 3D, then deliberately covered it over again.

research.summary: The Cochno Stone is a 12.8 x 7.9 m Bronze Age petroglyph panel at Auchnacraig, Faifley, West Dunbartonshire, with about 90 cup-and-ring indentations, recorded by the Rev. James Harvey in 1887. It was deliberately buried in 1965, on archaeologist Euan MacKie's recommendation, to stop vandalism. A trial dig in 2015 and a fuller two-week excavation in 2016, led by Dr Kenny Brophy of the University of Glasgow with the Factum Foundation, re-exposed and 3D-scanned it; the dig also revealed 19th- and 20th-century graffiti and painted lines made by Ludovic Maclellan Mann in 1937 while testing an eclipse-prediction theory that his own data went on to disprove. The stone was reburied after recording.

segments.narration: The oldest map of America was drawn with modern paint. Yale unveiled it in 1965, a day before Columbus Day, showing Vinland southwest of Greenland.
Paul Mellon had bought it for roughly three hundred thousand dollars and donated it, on one condition: total secrecy until the scholars published.
It looked unbeatable. So why did chemist after chemist keep finding a pigment no medieval scribe could possibly have owned?
The ink held anatase, a titanium dioxide manufactured only from the 1920s onward. Walter McCrone's team flagged it back in 1972.
Yale settled it in 2021. Titanium everywhere, almost no iron gall ink, and modern writing added to the real medieval manuscript bound beside it.

research.summary: The Vinland Map is a 20th-century forgery presented as a 15th-century mappa mundi showing Vinlanda Insula southwest of Greenland. It surfaced in 1957 bound with the genuine Tartar Relation, was sold for $3,500 to dealer Laurence C. Witten II, and was bought for about $300,000 by Yale alumnus Paul Mellon, who donated it on condition of secrecy until a scholarly book appeared; it was revealed the day before Columbus Day, 1965. Walter McCrone's team found anatase titanium dioxide in the ink in 1972, a pigment form made commercially only from the 1920s; Raman work by Brown and Clark confirmed it in 2002, and Yale's Richard Hark reported the same in 2018. Yale's 2021 X-ray fluorescence and Raman survey found titanium and barium throughout the ink lines with little to no iron, sulfur or copper, unlike genuine 15th-century manuscripts in the same collection, and infrared imaging showed the bound Tartar Relation had text altered in modern ink. Yale declared the map a forgery; it remains at the Beinecke Library.

segments.narration: A Maya book called fake for decades is the oldest. Ten bark-paper pages, an almanac tracking Venus, radiocarbon dated to between 1021 and 1154 AD.
Its arrival helped nobody believe it. A collector said he was flown in 1965 to an airstrip in Tabasco and shown the thing there.
No excavation records, no site, no paperwork at all. How do you ever prove a looted book is genuine?
Chemistry did it. Mexico's INAH found gypsum-prepared paper and pigments of lamp black, hematite red and Maya blue, all aged together with the sheets.
In 2018 INAH declared the codex authentic and renamed it the Codice Maya de Mexico, the oldest surviving book anywhere in the Americas.

research.summary: The Maya Codex of Mexico, long known as the Grolier Codex and renamed Codice Maya de Mexico by Mexico's INAH in 2018, is a pre-Columbian Maya screenfold almanac tracking Venus. Of an original 20 pages, 10 survive. It appeared in a private collection in the 1960s; Mexican collector Dr Josue Saenz said he was flown in 1965 to an airstrip near Tortuguero, Tabasco, and shown it, and it was first exhibited at the Grolier Club in New York from 20 April to 5 June 1971. Its authenticity was doubted from the start, partly for its looted, context-free origin, with J. Eric S. Thompson questioning it in 1975 without examining it. Radiocarbon tests gave 1035-1431 CE (1972), 1050-1284 CE (2012) and 1021-1154 CE (2018). Coe, Miller, Houston and Taube argued for authenticity in 2015, and in 2018 INAH-coordinated teams declared it authentic, citing gypsum-base paper preparation, pigments contemporaneous with the paper (lamp black, hematite red, Maya blue with palygorskite, cochineal browns) and at least three periods of high moisture, and confirming it as the oldest surviving book of the Americas.

segments.narration: Five hundred men worked fifteen years to build one hill. Silbury, in Wiltshire, stands thirty-nine metres high and holds 248,000 cubic metres of chalk.
That is eighteen million estimated man-hours, around 2400 BC. And almost no prehistoric artefacts have ever come out of it.
So people dug in anyway. A duke sank a shaft from the summit in 1776, and tunnels followed in 1849 and 1968.
The core gave up clay, flints, turf, antler tines and ox bones. Then in 2002 that 1776 shaft collapsed in heavy rain.
English Heritage backfilled the tunnels in 2007. Jim Leary and David Field concluded the point was never the finished mound, but the building of it.

research.summary: Silbury Hill, Wiltshire, part of the Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites World Heritage listing, is 39.3 m high with a 167 m base and a 30 m flat summit, containing about 248,000 cubic metres of earth and chalk, built in stages between roughly 2400 and 2300 BC. Archaeologists estimate 18 million man-hours, equivalent to 500 men working 15 years. It has been dug repeatedly: a vertical shaft sunk from the summit in October 1776 by Cornish miners under the Duke of Northumberland and Colonel Edward Drax, a horizontal tunnel in 1849, an east-side dig in 1867, and Richard J. C. Atkinson's 1968-1970 excavation. The core is mostly clay, flints, turf, gravel, shells, oak, hazel, sarsen stones, ox bones and antler tines, and few prehistoric artefacts have been found. The 1776 shaft collapsed in heavy rain in May 2002; English Heritage ran a seismic survey and in 2007-2008, with contractor Skanska, filled the tunnels and shafts with hundreds of tonnes of chalk while conducting a new survey. Jim Leary and David Field concluded in 2010 that the purpose cannot be known and that the building process may have mattered more than the finished mound.

segments.narration: Giant stone heads lie face-up on a Turkish mountain. Over two thousand metres up Nemrut, broken off statues that once stood nine metres tall.
King Antiochus of Commagene built this tomb-sanctuary in 62 BC: himself, two lions, two eagles, and gods who were half Greek, half Persian.
Behind the terraces rises a cone of loose rubble, forty-nine metres high. And the king's grave? Still missing.
That rubble is why. Dig into loose rock and the hole pours shut behind you, and archaeologists think that was the entire design.
A German engineer, Karl Sester, excavated here in 1881. Nearly a century and a half later, Antiochus is still somewhere inside his own mountain.

research.summary: Mount Nemrut in south-eastern Turkey, about 2,134 m high (the text also gives 2,150 m), carries the tomb-sanctuary King Antiochus I of Commagene built in 62 BC, with 8-9 m statues of himself, two lions, two eagles and composite Greek-Iranian gods. The statues' heads were removed at some point and are now scattered across the site, with nose damage suggesting deliberate iconoclasm. Behind the terraces is a tumulus of loose rock 49 m tall and 152 m in diameter; Wikipedia suggests it may have been built to protect the tomb from robbers, since any excavation would quickly fill in. The tomb of Antiochus I has never been found, though the site is still believed to be his burial place. Karl Sester, a German engineer surveying transport routes for the Ottomans, excavated the site in 1881; Theresa Goell first visited in 1947 and began campaigns in 1954. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

segments.narration: A temple vault in Kerala has stayed shut since the 1880s. Six chambers sit under Thiruvananthapuram's Padmanabhaswamy temple, labelled simply A to F.
In 2011 India's Supreme Court ordered five of them opened and inventoried. Vault A alone gave up over a hundred thousand objects.
Eight hundred kilos of gold coins, some of them struck around 200 BCE. And the sixth door simply stayed closed.
Not for want of a crowbar. A temple ritual in 2011 declared Vault B a forbidden zone, and the priests have opposed opening it ever since.
The court sided with custom. In July 2020 it handed control back to the former Travancore royal family, and Vault B is still sealed today.

research.summary: The Sree Padmanabhaswamy temple in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, has six known vaults (nilavaras) labelled A to F; a 2014 Amicus Curiae report mentions two further vaults, G and H, which remain unopened. In June 2011 the Supreme Court of India directed that the secret chambers be opened and their contents inventoried. Vaults A, C, D, E and F were opened with their antechambers; inventorying of C to F finished in August 2012 and formal inventorying of Vault A began at the end of 2012. Over 1.02 lakh articles came out of Vault A and its antechambers, and more than 2,000 from vaults C to F, including a hoard of about 800 kg of gold coins dating to around 200 BCE. Vault B is believed unopened since the 1880s: the royal family claimed opening it could be a bad omen, a four-day Ashtamangala Devaprasnam in August 2011 declared Kallara B a forbidden zone, and the Naduvil Madhom Pushpanjali Swamiyar opposed opening it in a letter dated 8 February 2016, though Amicus Curiae Gopal Subramanium recommended opening it in his April 2014 report. research.summary: Sigiriya is a massive column of granite about 180 metres high in central Sri Lanka, with a summit elevation of 349 metres. The Culavamsa credits King Kashyapa, given as CE 477 to 495 in the text and 473 to 491 in the article's royal template, with developing it into a city and fortress, and says he moved the capital to the secure summit to guard against the return of his half-brother Moggallana; Moggallana defeated him in 495 CE and moved the capital back to Anuradhapura, after which the site became a Buddhist monastery complex. Alternatives are recorded, including Dhatusena as primary builder and a reading in which the site had no military function. The Lion Gate sits on a plateau partway up, flanked by sculpted lion's paws, with a head above them that collapsed. Paintings would have covered an area of the western face 140 metres long and 40 metres high; a 2010 report refers to 22 frescoes, fading since 1930. The mirror wall is plastered brick, once polished enough to reflect the king, and Paranavithana deciphered 685 verses written on it between the 8th and 10th centuries, though the same article elsewhere refers to more than 1,500 poems and does not reconcile the two counts; the narration uses the lower, attributed figure. Sigiriya was inscribed by UNESCO in 1982 as the Ancient City of Sigiriya, reference 202. The UNESCO listing page and two secondary corroborating pages returned HTTP 403 from this environment, so every claim here rests on the Wikipedia article alone and the two internally inconsistent figures are flagged rather than resolved.

segments.narration: Iron Age islanders built a wall around a meteorite crater. Kaali, on Saaremaa, off the coast of Estonia.
The main crater is 110 metres wide and 22 metres deep, now filled with water. Eight smaller ones lie within a kilometre.
The rock came in at up to 20 kilometres a second and broke apart in the air. The blast was close to a small nuclear bomb.
And people were living there when it hit, though nobody agrees when that was, with estimates running from about 7,600 to 3,000 years ago. So what do you build after the sky explodes?
A 470-metre stone wall around the lake, with animal bones heaped inside, horses, sheep, oxen. Estonians called it the holy lake.

research.summary: Kaali is a field of nine meteorite craters at Kaali village on Saaremaa, Estonia. The main crater is 110 m across and 22 m deep and holds a lake; eight smaller craters, 12 to 40 m across and 1 to 4 m deep, lie within a kilometre. The meteoroid is estimated at 20 to 80 tonnes travelling 10 to 20 km/s, breaking up at 5 to 10 km altitude; the main fragment excavated about 81,000 cubic metres of dolomite and released roughly 80 TJ, about 20 kilotons of TNT, comparable to the Hiroshima bomb, incinerating vegetation within about 6 km. The dating is genuinely unsettled: Wikipedia's most recent estimate is shortly after 1530 to 1450 BC, but the same article records estimates from about 6,400 to about 400 years BCE, silicate spherules suggesting about 7,600 years, and an iridium signal pointing at the 4th century BC. A 2015 EGU abstract reports radiocarbon ages of 1800 to 1500 BC from post-impact sediments and argues they may underestimate the impact age, while a Moora et al. abstract favours 7600 plus or minus 50 radiocarbon years BP. The narration therefore gives a range and says nobody agrees. The site was populated at the time; 1976 to 1979 excavations found a fortified settlement to the north-east, with most finds from the pre-Roman Iron Age. The lake was probably enclosed in the early Iron Age by a stone wall about 470 m long, median width 2.5 m, average height 2.0 m, with many bones of horses, dogs, sheep, pigs and oxen inside it, possibly sacrifices; Wikipedia calls the site more of a cult site than a settlement and the lake a sacred lake, and it is traditionally known as the holy lake. Scholars including Karl Kello and Lennart Meri have linked the impact to Finnic mythology, including Kalevala runes 47 to 49; that link is a proposal, not a settled finding, and the narration does not assert it.
